title: Is the Indianapolis Housing Market Slowing Down Heading Into Winter?
hook: Heading into winter, the Indianapolis-area housing market is slower and roomier than it was a year ago: more listings, longer market times and slightly lower asking prices.
body:
# Is the Indianapolis Housing Market Slowing Down Heading Into Winter?

Heading into winter, the Indianapolis-area housing market is slower and roomier than it was a year ago: more listings, longer market times and slightly lower asking prices. Realtor.com's October 2026 figures show 7,171 homes for sale across the Indianapolis-Carmel-Anderson metro, 21.3% more than a year earlier. Hamilton County is following the same path at a higher price point.

## What do the October 2026 numbers show?

| Metric | Area | Oct 2026 | Oct 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active listings | Indy metro | 7,171 | 5,910 |
| Active listings | Hamilton County | 1,111 | 931 |
| Median list price | Indy metro | $305,000 | $320,000 |
| Median list price | Hamilton County | $445,000 | $475,000 |
| Median days on market | Indy metro | 55 | 50 |
| Pending listings | Indy metro | 2,651 | 3,011 |
| Share of listings with a price cut | Indy metro | 55.4% | 62.2% |

*Source: Realtor.com via FRED, October 2026. Prices are median list prices (what sellers asked), not sale prices. The price-cut share is listings with a reduction divided by active listings.*

## Why are there so many more homes for sale?

Homes are staying on the market longer, so they pile up. Fewer homes went under contract this October than last, and the typical listing sat about five days longer. Mortgage rates are also higher than a year ago, which trims what many buyers can comfortably spend each month.

Part of this is the season. New listings and pending sales slow every late fall and winter in the Realtor.com series. What is different this year is the starting point: the metro has more homes for sale than at any time in the past two years of data.

## Are home prices going down in the Indianapolis area?

Asking prices are a little lower, not falling off a cliff. The metro median list price is down 4.7% from a year ago. Medians also move with the mix of homes on the market, so a dip does not mean every home lost value. List prices tell you what sellers are asking. For what a specific home is worth, recent sales of similar homes nearby matter far more.

## Are more sellers cutting prices?

Fewer, as a share of the market. In October, 55.4% of metro listings had a price reduction, down from 62.2% a year earlier.

That surprises people, because the market feels softer. Here is the plain-English read: inventory grew faster than price cuts did, so a smaller slice of listings needed one. That suggests more sellers are pricing closer to the market from the start. Price cuts are still common, though. More than half of listings had one, so buyers can expect some room to negotiate on homes that have been sitting.

## How is Hamilton County different from the metro?

Fishers, Carmel, Noblesville and Westfield are showing the same trend at a higher price point. Hamilton County had 1,111 active listings in October, up 19.3% from a year earlier, and its median list price was lower than last October. Homes there still tend to move a little faster than the metro as a whole.

County figures blend very different neighborhoods, so treat them as the backdrop, not a forecast for one street.

## What this means for buyers

- **More choice.** You can compare several homes instead of racing to the first one.
- **More time.** Longer market times leave room to ask for repairs, credits or a flexible closing date.
- **Payment first.** Get pre-approved and settle on a monthly payment you are comfortable with before you tour.

## What this means for sellers

- **Expect competition.** Buyers can see more alternatives than they could a year ago.
- **Price for today.** Compare your home with what is for sale now, not with last spring's asking prices.
- **Presentation counts.** In a slower season, homes that are clean, repaired and well photographed stand out.
- **Allow extra time.** Build some cushion into your moving plans.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is it a buyer's market in the Indianapolis area right now?

It has shifted toward buyers compared with a year ago, with more listings, fewer pending sales and longer market times. Higher mortgage rates offset part of that advantage, so the market rewards preparation on both sides.

### Will Indianapolis home prices keep falling this winter?

No one can say for sure. In the Realtor.com series, the metro median list price dipped during each of the last two winters and rose again in spring. That pattern is a guide, not a promise.

### Does the Realtor.com data show what homes sold for?

No. These figures track listings: asking prices, inventory, pending sales, price cuts and days on market. For sold prices in your neighborhood, ask a local agent for a comparative market analysis.

## How do these trends apply to your home?

Market statistics provide the starting point, not the complete answer. Your price range, neighborhood and timeline shape what these trends mean for you. Ask the Evelo Team for a winter market check on your price range: call 317-863-9011 or email info@eveloteam.com.

title: Should You Sell Your Hamilton County Home in Winter or Wait for Spring?
hook: Winter can be a good time to sell in Hamilton County if your home is ready and your timeline is firm.
body:
# Should You Sell Your Hamilton County Home in Winter or Wait for Spring?

Winter can be a good time to sell in Hamilton County if your home is ready and your timeline is firm. Spring, though, has brought faster sales and higher asking prices in each of the past two years. The better choice depends less on the calendar and more on your timeline, your next move and the homes you would be competing with.

## What does the latest data say about selling in Hamilton County?

| Metric | Area | Oct 2026 | Oct 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median list price | Hamilton County | $445,000 | $475,000 |
| Active listings | Hamilton County | 1,111 | 931 |
| Median days on market | Hamilton County | 49 | 45 |
| Pending listings | Indy metro | 2,651 | 3,011 |

*Source: Realtor.com via FRED, October 2026. Prices are median list prices (what sellers asked), not sale prices. Pending listings are reported for the whole Indianapolis-Carmel-Anderson metro.*

Two things stand out. Hamilton County's median list price is down 6.3% from a year ago, yet it still sits 45.9% above the metro median. And the county now holds 15.5% of all homes for sale in the metro, so sellers here face more competition than they did last fall.

## What are the advantages of selling in winter?

- **Fewer competing listings, usually.** Hamilton County's inventory fell through each of the last two winters in the Realtor.com data, then climbed again in spring and summer.
- **Buyers with a reason to move.** People shopping in December and January are often working around a job change, a lease ending or another firm deadline.
- **You move on your schedule.** If you have already found your next home, waiting has real costs: mortgage payments, property taxes, utilities and upkeep.
- **Your purchase may be easier too.** If you are selling to buy in Fishers, Carmel, Noblesville or Westfield, you would be buying in the same quieter market.

## What are the drawbacks of selling in winter?

- **Fewer buyers.** Pending sales across the metro were lower this October than last, and in each of the past two years they hit their low point in January.
- **More time on the market.** Days on market in Hamilton County climbed every winter in the data, then dropped sharply by March.
- **More competition than last winter.** With inventory well above a year ago, the usual winter dip may still leave plenty of homes for buyers to compare.
- **Weather and holidays.** Snow, short days and the holiday calendar make showings, photos and curb appeal harder.
- **Higher rates.** Mortgage rates are higher than a year ago, which trims what some buyers can spend.

## What does waiting for spring really get you?

In both of the past two years, Hamilton County's median list price rose from December into spring, and days on market fell well below winter levels. That is a real advantage.

But spring is not a sure thing:

- **More sellers show up too.** New listings climb sharply each spring, so you would compete with more homes.
- **Asking prices have been easing.** Any spring rise would start from a lower base than last year's.
- **Rates are unpredictable.** No one can promise where mortgage rates will be in April.
- **Waiting costs money.** Every extra month you own the home adds carrying costs.

## Why does pricing matter more than timing?

Price cuts happen in every season. A home priced in line with its competition from the first day has a better chance of avoiding the cycle of sitting, cutting and sitting again, whether it lists in January or April. A pricing review based on recent comparable sales nearby will tell you more than any seasonal average.

## What this means for sellers

- **Consider winter** if your home is ready, your timeline is firm, or you have already found your next place.
- **Consider spring** if you have flexibility, your home needs work, or you want the most buyer traffic and can handle more competition.
- **Either way,** use the winter months for small repairs, decluttering and a pricing review.

## What this means for buyers

- **Winter can work in your favor.** Owners who list in winter often have a reason to move, which can open room to talk about price, repairs or closing dates.
- **Get ready early.** Pre-approval before the holidays lets you act when the right home appears.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do homes sell for less in the winter?

The Realtor.com data tracks asking prices, not sale prices. Hamilton County's median list price has been lower in winter than in spring over the past two years, but that median also reflects which homes happen to be listed. Your own price depends on recent comparable sales nearby.

### How long does it take to sell a home in Hamilton County right now?

The median was 49 days on market in October 2026, up from 45 a year earlier. Price, condition and location make a big difference for any one home.

### If I want to sell in spring, when should I start?

Earlier than you might think. Many sellers use January and February for repairs, staging and a pricing review, so the home is ready when buyer activity picks up.

## Not sure which season fits your plans?

The timing should be yours, and so should the pace. One Fishers client described her experience with the team this way: "They never tried to upsell or pressure us to move faster than we were comfortable. They listen and care about their clients." (Natalie, buyer in Fishers; review published on eveloteam.com)
